entity_title: Authorisation to stay must precede entry
fact_text: A third-country salaried worker must obtain a temporary authorisation to stay from the General Department of immigration BEFORE travelling to Luxembourg; an application filed from inside Luxembourg is rejected as inadmissible.
evidence_quote: Applications submitted from Luxembourg are inadmissible

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can move to Luxembourg first and arrange work authorisation once there. Actually a third-country national must have the temporary authorisation to stay approved before entry, and applications lodged from inside the country are inadmissible. Action: apply to the General Department of immigration from your country of residence before booking travel.

entity_title: 90-day validity of the authorisation to stay
fact_text: The temporary authorisation to stay is valid for only 90 days, within which the visa-required worker must obtain a type D visa and/or enter Luxembourg and make the declaration of arrival.
evidence_quote: This temporary authorisation to stay is valid for a duration of 90 days

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the approved authorisation to stay is an open-ended green light to relocate. Actually it is valid for just 90 days, in which the visa and entry steps must be completed. Action: schedule the type D visa application and travel immediately after the authorisation arrives by post.

entity_title: Type D long-stay visa follows the authorisation
fact_text: Visa-required third-country nationals must apply for a type D long-stay visa from their country of origin AFTER obtaining the temporary authorisation to stay; the visa is a separate step that follows, not replaces, the authorisation.
evidence_quote: they must apply for a type D visa before their trip and from their country of origin

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a single visa covers a move to work in Luxembourg. Actually visa-nationals need a type D long-stay visa applied for abroad, and only after the temporary authorisation to stay has been granted. Action: obtain the authorisation first, then lodge the type D visa at the Luxembourg (or representing Belgian/Dutch) mission before travel.

fact_text: After entering Luxembourg a third-country salaried worker must apply for the residence permit within 3 months of entry; the authorisation to stay does not substitute for the permit.
evidence_quote: within 3 months of entry into Luxembourg

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the visa or authorisation to stay is enough to live and work long-term. Actually the residence permit is a distinct document that must be applied for within 3 months of entering Luxembourg. Action: file the residence permit application on MyGuichet.lu (or by post) within three months of arrival.

entity_title: Declaration of arrival doubles as interim work permit
fact_text: A third-country worker must make a declaration of arrival at their commune of residence; the stamped copy together with the temporary authorisation to stay serves as the interim work permit and residence proof until the residence permit card is issued.
evidence_quote: The copy of the declaration of arrival together with the authorisation to stay both serve as a work permit and authorisation to stay until the residence permit is issued

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you cannot legally start work until the residence permit card arrives. Actually the commune's declaration-of-arrival receipt plus the authorisation to stay together act as a valid work permit in the interim. Action: register at the commune promptly and keep the receipt with the authorisation to stay as proof of the right to work.

fact_text: A non-EU salaried worker must undergo a medical check for foreigners (examination plus tuberculosis screening); the resulting medical certificate from the Health Directorate is required before the residence permit application can be processed.
evidence_quote: The non-EU national salaried worker must undergo a medical check for foreigners as soon as possible

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed no health formalities are needed once a job is secured. Actually non-EU workers must complete a medical check for foreigners, including a TB screening, and the certificate gates the residence permit. Action: book the medical examination and TB screening (laboratory or Ligue medico-sociale) as soon as you arrive.

entity_title: Employer must clear the ADEM labour-market test
fact_text: Before a third-country national's authorisation to stay can be granted, the employer must run the ADEM labour-market test and obtain the original ADEM certificate authorising the hire; the worker must attach that original certificate to their application.
evidence_quote: be in possession of the original certificate issued by the National Employment Agency (ADEM) authorising the employer to hire a third-country national

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a signed job offer is sufficient to be hired from abroad. Actually the employer must first declare the vacancy to ADEM, wait out the labour-market test, and obtain an original certificate authorising the third-country hire, which the worker must attach to the authorisation-to-stay application. Action: confirm the employer has secured the original ADEM certificate before applying.

entity_title: First permit tied to one profession and one sector
fact_text: The first residence permit for a third-country salaried worker is valid for a maximum of one year and only for one profession (with all employers) in a single sector, encoded as an ISCO code; changing sector or profession needs ministerial authorisation.
evidence_quote: for one profession only with all employers

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a work-based permit lets you take any job in Luxembourg. Actually the first residence permit is limited to one profession and one sector (shown as an ISCO code) and lasts at most one year; a change needs the Minister's authorisation. Action: verify the target job's sector/profession matches the permit before switching roles or employers.

fact_text: To qualify for the EU Blue Card as a highly qualified third-country worker, the job must offer an annual salary at least equal to the amount set by Grand-Ducal regulation (currently EUR 65,652) on a contract of at least 6 months.
evidence_quote: be offered an annual salary at least equal to the amount set by Grand-Ducal regulation (EUR 65,652)

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed any well-paid professional automatically gets the EU Blue Card. Actually there is a statutory minimum annual salary set by Grand-Ducal regulation (currently EUR 65,652) plus a contract of at least 6 months and proof of high qualifications. Action: confirm the gross annual salary meets the current Grand-Ducal threshold before choosing the Blue Card route.

entity_title: CCSS affiliation certificate needed to renew
fact_text: To renew the residence permit, a third-country salaried worker must supply a recent CCSS (Joint Social Security Centre) certificate of affiliation listing all their social-security affiliations, evidencing continuous lawful employment.
evidence_quote: a recent certificate of affiliation which must include all the salaried worker's affiliations to the social security

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed renewing a residence permit is a formality once you are employed. Actually renewal requires a recent CCSS certificate of affiliation covering all your social-security affiliations to prove you actually worked. Action: order the affiliation certificate from the CCSS before filing the renewal, two months ahead of expiry.

entity_title: Biometric card that also carries the work permit
fact_text: The third-country residence permit is issued as a biometric chip card that also embeds the work permit; there is no separate work-permit document, so the residence card itself proves the right to work.
evidence_quote: The residence permit takes the form of a chip card containing the biometric data. It also contains the work permit

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a residence permit and a work permit are two separate documents. Actually the Luxembourg third-country residence permit is a single biometric chip card that also contains the work permit. Action: treat the residence permit card as your combined right-to-reside and right-to-work document for employers and authorities.

fact_text: The third-country residence permit application requires proof of payment of an EUR 80 fee to the Ministry of Home Affairs (General Department of immigration); the same EUR 80 fee is payable again at each renewal.
evidence_quote: proof of payment of a fee of EUR 80 to account IBAN LU46 1111 2582 2814 0000

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the residence permit is issued free once approved. Actually proof of an EUR 80 payment to the immigration department's account must accompany the application, and it recurs at every renewal. Action: pay the EUR 80 fee to the stated IBAN and attach the payment proof to the application.
